entries.10b203f31d061c544fd4263a575e5aea883048f3: <div sID="gen19436" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="5" osisID="Dan.5" sID="Dan.5"/> <div eID="gen19436" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19437" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen19438" type="x-p"/> The destruction of the kingdom of Babylon had been long and often foretold when it was at a distance; in this chapter we have it accomplished, and a prediction of it the very same night that it was accomplished. Belshazzar now reigned in Babylon; some compute he had reigned seventeen years, others but three; we have here the story of his exit and the period of his kingdom. We must know that about two years before this Cyrus king of Persia, a growing monarch, came against Babylon with a great army; Belshazzar met him, fought him, and was routed by him in a pitched battle. He and his scattered forces retired into the city, where Cyrus besieged them. They were very secure, because the river Euphrates was their bulwark, and they had twenty years; provision in the city; but in the second year of the siege he took it, as is here related. We have in this chapter, I. The riotous, idolatrous, sacrilegious feast which Belshazzar made, in which he filled up the measure of his iniquity, <reference osisRef="Dan.5.1-Dan.5.4">ver. 1-4</reference>. II. The alarm given him in the midst of his jollity by a hand-writing on the wall, which none of his wise men could read or tell him the meaning of, <reference osisRef="Dan.5.5-Dan.5.9">ver. 5-9</reference>. III. The interpretation of the mystical characters by Daniel, who was at length brought in to him, and dealt plainly with him, and showed him his doom written, <reference osisRef="Dan.5.10-Dan.5.28">ver. 10-28</reference>. IV. The immediate accomplishment of the interpretation in the slaying of the king and seizing of the kingdom, <reference osisRef="Dan.5.30-Dan.5.31">ver. 30, 31</reference>.
entries.18dac8b1fef61a44fd3fb6a4224a443bbc775fbd: <div eID="gen19438" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen19437" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Belshazzar's Feast; The Hand-writing on the Wall. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 538.)</title> <div sID="gen19439" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Belshazzar the king made a great feast to a thousand of his lords, and drank wine before the thousand. <hi type="super">2</hi> Belshazzar, whiles he tasted the wine, commanded to bring the golden and silver vessels which his father Nebuchadnezzar had taken out of the temple which <hi type="italic">was</hi> in Jerusalem; that the king, and his princes, his wives, and his concubines, might drink therein. <hi type="super">3</hi> Then they brought the golden vessels that were taken out of the temple of the house of God which <hi type="italic">was</hi> at Jerusalem; and the king, and his princes, his wives, and his concubines, drank in them. <hi type="super">4</hi> They drank wine, and praised the gods of gold, and of silver, of brass, of iron, of wood, and of stone. <hi type="super">5</hi> In the same hour came forth fingers of a man's hand, and wrote over against the candlestick upon the plaster of the wall of the king's palace: and the king saw the part of the hand that wrote. <hi type="super">6</hi> Then the king's countenance was changed, and his thoughts troubled him, so that the joints of his loins were loosed, and his knees smote one against another. <hi type="super">7</hi> The king cried aloud to bring in the astrologers, the Chaldeans, and the soothsayers. <hi type="italic">And</hi> the king spake, and said to the wise <hi type="italic">men</hi> of Babylon, Whosoever shall read this writing, and show me the interpretation thereof, shall be clothed with scarlet, and <hi type="italic">have</hi> a chain of gold about his neck, and shall be the third ruler in the kingdom. <hi type="super">8</hi> Then came in all the king's wise <hi type="italic">men:</hi> but they could not read the writing, nor make known to the king the interpretation thereof. <hi type="super">9</hi> Then was king Belshazzar greatly troubled, and his countenance was changed in him, and his lords were astonied. <div eID="gen19439" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19440" type="x-p"/> We have here Belshazzar the king very gay, but all of a sudden very gloomy, and in straits in the fulness of his sufficiency. See how he affronts God, and God affrights him; and wait what will be the issue of this contest; and whether he that hardened his heart against God prospered. <div eID="gen19440" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19441" type="x-p"/> I. See how the king affronted God, and put contempt upon him. He <hi type="italic">made a great feast,</hi> or <hi type="italic">banquet of wine;</hi> probably it was some anniversary solemnity, in honour of his birth-day or coronation-day, or in honour of some of their idols. Historians say that Cyrus, who was now with his army besieging Babylon, knew of this feast, and presuming that they then would be off their guard, <hi type="italic">somno vinoque sepulti—buried in sleep and wine,</hi> took that opportunity to attack the city, and so with the more ease made himself master of it. Belshazzar upon this occasion invited <hi type="italic">a thousand of his lords</hi> to come and drink with him. Perhaps they were such as had signalized themselves in defense of the city against the besiegers; or these were his great council of war, with whom, when they had well drunk, he would advise what was further to be done. And they were to look upon it as a great favour that he <hi type="italic">drank wine before</hi> them, for it was the pride of those eastern kings to be seldom seen. He drank wine before them, for he made this feast, as Ahasuerus did, to show the <hi type="italic">honour of his majesty.</hi> Now in this sumptuous feast, 1. He put an affront upon the providence of God and bade defiance to his judgments. His city was now besieged; a powerful enemy was at his gates; his life and kingdom lay at stake. In all this the hand of the Lord had gone out against him, and by it he called him to <hi type="italic">weeping, and mourning, and girding with sackcloth.</hi> God's voice cried in the city, as Jonah to Nineveh, <hi type="italic">Yet forty days,</hi> or fewer, <hi type="italic">and Babylon shall be destroyed.</hi> He should therefore, like the king of Nineveh, have proclaimed a fast; but, as one resolved to walk contrary to God, he proclaims a feast, and behold <hi type="italic">joy and gladness, slaying oxen, killing sheep, eating flesh, and drinking wine,</hi> as if he dared the Almighty to do his worst, <reference osisRef="Isa.22.12-Isa.22.13">Isa. xxii. 12, 13</reference>. To show how little fear he had of being forced to surrender, for want of provisions, he spent thus extravagantly. Note, Security and sensuality are sad presages of approaching ruin. Those that will not be warned by judgments of God may expect to be wounded by them. 2. He put an affront upon the temple of God, and bade defiance to his sanctuary, <reference osisRef="Dan.6.2">v. 2</reference>. <hi type="italic">While he tasted the wine, he commanded to bring the vessels of</hi> the temple, that they might drink in them. When he tasted how rich and fine the wine was, "O," said he, "it is a pity but we should have holy vessels to drink such delicious wine as this in," which was looked upon as a piece of wit, and, to carry on the humour, the vessels of the temple were immediately sent for. Nay, there seems to have been something more in it than a frolic, and that it was done in a malicious despite to the God of Israel. The heart of his people was very much upon these sacred vessels, as appears from <reference osisRef="Jer.27.16">Jer. xxvii. 16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.27.18">18</reference>. Their principal care, at their return, was about these, <reference osisRef="Ezra.1.7">Ezra i. 7</reference>. Now, we may suppose, they had an expectation of their deliverance approaching, reckoning the seventy years of their captivity near a period; and some of them might perhaps have given out some words to that purport, that shortly they should have the vessels of the sanctuary restored to them, in defiance of which Belshazzar here proclaims them to be his own, will keep them in store no longer, but will make use of them among his own plate. Note, That mirth is sinful indeed, and fills the measure of men's iniquity apace, which profanes sacred things and jests with them. This ripened Babylon for ruin—that no songs would serve them but the <hi type="italic">songs of Zion</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.137.3">Ps. cxxxvii. 3</reference>), no vessels but the vessels of the sanctuary. Let those who thus sacrilegiously alienate what is dedicated to God and his honour know that he <hi type="italic">will not be mocked.</hi> 3. He put an affront upon God himself, and bade defiance to his deity; for <hi type="italic">they drank wine, and praised the gods of gold and silver,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.6.4">v. 4</reference>. They gave that glory to images, the work of their own hands and creatures of their own fancy, which is due to the true and living God only. They praised them either with sacrifices offered to them or with songs sung in honour of them. When their heads were giddy, and their hearts merry, with wine, they were in the fittest frame to <hi type="italic">praise the gods of gold and silver, wood and stone;</hi> for one would think that men in their senses, who had the command of a clear and sober thought, could not be guilty of so gross an absurdity; they must be intoxicated ere they could be so infatuated. Drunken worshippers, who are not men, but beasts, are the most proper for the service of dunghill deities, that are not gods, but devils. <hi type="italic">They have erred through wine,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.27.7">Isa. xxvii. 7</reference>. They drank wine, and praised their idol-gods, as if they had been the founders of their feast and the givers of all good things to them. Or, when they were drinking wine, they praised their gods by drinking healths to them; and the king <hi type="italic">drank wine before</hi> them (<reference osisRef="Dan.6.1">v. 1</reference>), that is, he began the health, first to this god, and then to the other, till they went through the <hi type="italic">bead-roll</hi> or <hi type="italic">farrago</hi> of them, those of <hi type="italic">wood and stone</hi> not excepted. Note, Immorality and impiety, vice and profaneness, strengthen the hands and advance the interests one of another. Drunken frolics were an introduction to idolatry, and then idolatrous healths were a shoeing-horn to further drunkenness. <div eID="gen19441" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19442" type="x-p"/> II. See how God affrighted the king, and struck a terror upon him. Belshazzar and his lords are in the midst of their revels, the cups going round apace, and all upon the merry pin, drinking confusion, it may be, to Cyrus and his army, and roaring out huzzas, in confidence of the speedy raising of the siege; but the hour had come when that must be fulfilled which had been long ago said of the king of Babylon, when his city should be besieged by the Persians and Medes, <reference osisRef="Isa.21.2-Isa.21.4">Isa. xxi. 2-4</reference>. <hi type="italic">The night of my pleasures has he turned into fear to me.</hi> The mirth of this ball at court must be spoiled, and a damp cast upon their jollity, though the king himself be master of the revels; immediately, when God speaks the word, we have him and all his guests in the utmost confusion, and the end of their mirth is heaviness. 1. There appear the <hi type="italic">fingers of a man's hand writing on the plaster of the wall,</hi> before the king's face (<reference osisRef="Dan.6.5">v. 5</reference>), "the angel Gabriel," say the rabbin, "directing these fingers and writing by them." "That divine hand" (says a rabbi of our own, Dr. Lightfoot) "that had written the two tables for a law to his people now writes the doom of Babel and Belshazzar upon the wall." Here was nothing sent to frighten them which made a noise, or threatened their lives, no claps of thunder nor flashes of lightning, no destroying angel with his sword drawn in his hand, only a pen in the hand, writing upon the wall, <hi type="italic">over-against the candlestick,</hi> where they might all see it by the light of their own candle. Note, God's written word is sufficient to put the proudest boldest sinners into a fright, when he is pleased to give it the setting on. The king saw <hi type="italic">the part of the hand that wrote,</hi> but saw not the person whose hand it was, which made the thing more frightful. Note, What we see of God, the part of the hand that writes in the book of the creatures and the book of the scriptures (<hi type="italic">Lo, these are parts of his ways,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.26.14">Job xxvi. 14</reference>), may serve to possess us with awful thoughts concerning that of God which we do not see. If this be <hi type="italic">the finger of God,</hi> what is his arm made bare? And what is he? 2. The king is immediately seized with a panic fear (<reference osisRef="Dan.6.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">His countenance was changed</hi> (his colour went and came); <hi type="italic">the joints of his loins were loosed,</hi> so that he had no strength in them, but was struck with a pain in his back, as is usual in a great fright; <hi type="italic">his knees smote one against another,</hi> so violently did he tremble like an aspen leaf. But what was the matter? Why is he in such a fright? He perceives not what is written, and how does he know but it may be some happy presage of deliverance to him and to his kingdom? But the business was <hi type="italic">his thoughts troubled him;</hi> his own guilty conscience flew in his face, and told him that he had no reason to expect any good news from Heaven, and that the hand of an angel could write nothing but terror to him. He that knew himself liable to the justice of God immediately concluded this to be an arrest in his name, a summons to appear before him. Note, God can soon awaken the most secure and make the heart of the stoutest sinner to tremble; and there needs no more to do it than to let loose his own thoughts upon him; they will soon play the tyrant, and give him trouble enough. 3. The wise men of Babylon are immediately called in, to see what they can make of this writing upon the wall, <reference osisRef="Dan.6.7">v. 7</reference>. The king <hi type="italic">cried aloud,</hi> as one in haste, as one in earnest, to bring the whole college of magicians, to try if they can <hi type="italic">read this writing,</hi> and <hi type="italic">show the interpretation of it;</hi> for the king and all his lords cannot pretend to it, it is out of their sphere. The study of divine revelation (such as they had, or thought they had) and converse with the world of spirits were by the heathen confined to one profession, and no other meddled with it; but what is written to us by the finger of God is legible to all; whoever will may read the mind of God in the scriptures. To engage these wise men to exert the utmost of their skill in this matter, and provoke them to an emulation in the attempt, he promised that whoever would give him a satisfactory account of this writing should be dignified with the highest honours of the court. He knew what these pretenders to wisdom aimed at, and what would please them, and therefore promised them a <hi type="italic">scarlet robe</hi> and a <hi type="italic">gold chain,</hi> glorious things in the eyes of those that know no better. Nay, he should be <hi type="italic">primus par regni—chief minister of state, the third ruler</hi> in the kingdom, next to the king and his heir apparent. 4. The king is disappointed in his expectations from them; they can none of them <hi type="italic">read the writing,</hi> much less interpret it (<reference osisRef="Dan.6.8">v. 8</reference>), which increases the king's confusion, <reference osisRef="Dan.6.9">v. 9</reference>. He likes the thing yet worse and worse, and fears that mischief is towards him. <hi type="italic">His lords</hi> also, that had been partners with him in his jollity, are now sharers with him in his terrors; they also were <hi type="italic">astonished</hi> at their wits' end; and neither their numbers nor their refreshment by wine would serve to keep up their spirits. The reason why the wise men could not read the writing was not because it was written in any language or characters unknown to them, but God either cast a mist before their eyes or put such confusion upon their spirits that they could not read it, that the honour of expounding this mystical writing might be reserved for Daniel. Note, The terror of an awakened convinced conscience may justly be increased by the utter insufficiency of all creatures to give it ease or satisfaction.
entries.c9d53b5fb47d36956503e464ce470d80b360c691: <div eID="gen19442" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Daniel Brought before Belshazzar. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 538.)</title> <div sID="gen19443" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> <hi type="italic">Now</hi> the queen, by reason of the words of the king and his lords, came into the banquet house: <hi type="italic">and</hi> the queen spake and said, O king, live for ever: let not thy thoughts trouble thee, nor let thy countenance be changed: <hi type="super">11</hi> There is a man in thy kingdom, in whom <hi type="italic">is</hi> the spirit of the holy gods; and in the days of thy father light and understanding and wisdom, like the wisdom of the gods, was found in him; whom the king Nebuchadnezzar thy father, the king, <hi type="italic">I say,</hi> thy father, made master of the magicians, astrologers, Chaldeans, <hi type="italic">and</hi> soothsayers; <hi type="super">12</hi> Forasmuch as an excellent spirit, and knowledge, and understanding, interpreting of dreams, and showing of hard sentences, and dissolving of doubts, were found in the same Daniel, whom the king named Belteshazzar: now let Daniel be called, and he will show the interpretation. <hi type="super">13</hi> Then was Daniel brought in before the king. <hi type="italic">And</hi> the king spake and said unto Daniel, <hi type="italic">Art</hi> thou that Daniel, which <hi type="italic">art</hi> of the children of the captivity of Judah, whom the king my father brought out of Jewry? <hi type="super">14</hi> I have even heard of thee, that the spirit of the gods <hi type="italic">is</hi> in thee, and <hi type="italic">that</hi> light and understanding and excellent wisdom is found in thee. <hi type="super">15</hi> And now the wise <hi type="italic">men,</hi> the astrologers, have been brought in before me, that they should read this writing, and make known unto me the interpretation thereof: but they could not show the interpretation of the thing: <hi type="super">16</hi> And I have heard of thee, that thou canst make interpretations, and dissolve doubts: now if thou canst read the writing, and make known to me the interpretation thereof, thou shalt be clothed with scarlet, and <hi type="italic">have</hi> a chain of gold about thy neck, and shalt be the third ruler in the kingdom. <hi type="super">17</hi> Then Daniel answered and said before the king, Let thy gifts be to thyself, and give thy rewards to another; yet I will read the writing unto the king, and make known to him the interpretation. <hi type="super">18</hi> O thou king, the most high God gave Nebuchadnezzar thy father a kingdom, and majesty, and glory, and honour: <hi type="super">19</hi> And for the majesty that he gave him, all people, nations, and languages, trembled and feared before him: whom he would he slew; and whom he would he kept alive; and whom he would he set up; and whom he would he put down. <hi type="super">20</hi> But when his heart was lifted up, and his mind hardened in pride, he was deposed from his kingly throne, and they took his glory from him: <hi type="super">21</hi> And he was driven from the sons of men; and his heart was made like the beasts, and his dwelling <hi type="italic">was</hi> with the wild asses: they fed him with grass like oxen, and his body was wet with the dew of heaven; till he knew that the most high God ruled in the kingdom of men, and <hi type="italic">that</hi> he appointeth over it whomsoever he will. <hi type="super">22</hi> And thou his son, O Belshazzar, hast not humbled thine heart, though thou knewest all this; <hi type="super">23</hi> But hast lifted up thyself against the Lord of heaven; and they have brought the vessels of his house before thee, and thou, and thy lords, thy wives, and thy concubines, have drunk wine in them; and thou hast praised the gods of silver, and gold, of brass, iron, wood, and stone, which see not, nor hear, nor know: and the God in whose hand thy breath <hi type="italic">is,</hi> and whose <hi type="italic">are</hi> all thy ways, hast thou not glorified: <hi type="super">24</hi> Then was the part of the hand sent from him; and this writing was written. <hi type="super">25</hi> And this <hi type="italic">is</hi> the writing that was written, MENE, MENE, TEKEL, UPHARSIN. <hi type="super">26</hi> This <hi type="italic">is</hi> the interpretation of the thing: MENE; God hath numbered thy kingdom, and finished it. <hi type="super">27</hi> TEKEL; Thou art weighed in the balances, and art found wanting. <hi type="super">28</hi> PERES; Thy kingdom is divided, and given to the Medes and Persians. <hi type="super">29</hi> Then commanded Belshazzar, and they clothed Daniel with scarlet, and <hi type="italic">put</hi> a chain of gold about his neck, and made a proclamation concerning him, that he should be the third ruler in the kingdom. <div eID="gen19443" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19444" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. The information given to the king, by the queen-mother, concerning Daniel, how fit he was to be consulted in this difficult case. It is supposed that this queen was the widow of Evil-Merodach, and was that famous Nitocris whom Herodotus mentions as a woman of extraordinary prudence. She was not present at the feast, as the king's <hi type="italic">wives and concubines were</hi> (<reference osisRef="Dan.6.2">v. 2</reference>); it was not agreeable to her age and gravity to keep a merry night. But, tidings of the fright which the king and his lords were put into being brought to her apartment, she came herself to the banqueting-house, to recommend to the king a physician for his melancholy. She entreated him not to be discouraged by the insufficiency of his wise men to solve this riddle, for that there was <hi type="italic">a man in his kingdom</hi> that had more than once helped his grandfather at such a dead lift, and, no doubt, could help him, <reference osisRef="Dan.6.11-Dan.6.12">v. 11, 12</reference>. She could not undertake to read the writing herself, but directed him to one that could; let <hi type="italic">Daniel be called</hi> now, who should have been called first. Now observe, 1. The high character she gives of Daniel: He is a <hi type="italic">man in whom is the spirit of the holy gods,</hi> who has something in him more than human, not only the <hi type="italic">spirit of a man,</hi> which, in all, is the <hi type="italic">candle of the Lord,</hi> but a divine spirit. According to the language of her country and religion, she could not give a higher encomium of any man; she speaks honourably of him as a man that had, (1.) An admirably good head: <hi type="italic">Light, and understanding, and wisdom, like the wisdom of the gods, were found in him.</hi> Such an insight had he into things secret, and such a foresight of things to come, that it was evident he was divinely inspired; he had <hi type="italic">knowledge</hi> and <hi type="italic">understanding</hi> beyond all the other wise men for <hi type="italic">interpreting dreams,</hi> explaining enigmas or hard sentences, untying knots, and resolving doubts. Solomon had a wonderful sagacity of this kind; but it should seem that in these things Daniel had more of an immediate divine direction. <hi type="italic">Behold, a greater than Solomon</hi> himself <hi type="italic">is here.</hi> Yet what was the wisdom of them both compared with the treasures of wisdom hidden in Christ? (2.) He had an admirably good heart: <hi type="italic">An excellent spirit was found in him,</hi> which was a great ornament to his wisdom and knowledge, and qualified him to receive that gift; for God <hi type="italic">gives to a man that is good in his sight wisdom, and knowledge, and joy.</hi> He was of a humble, holy, heavenly spirit, had a devout and gracious spirit, a spirit of zeal for the glory of God and the good of men. This was indeed an excellent spirit. 2. The account she gives of the respect that Nebuchadnezzar had for him; he was much in his favour, and was preferred by him: "<hi type="italic">The king thy father"</hi> (that is, thy grandfather, but even to many generations Nebuchadnezzar might well be called the father of that royal family, for he it was that raised it to such a pitch of grandeur), "<hi type="italic">the king,</hi> I say, <hi type="italic">thy father, made him master of the magicians.</hi>" Perhaps Belshazzar had sometimes, in his pride, spoken slightly of Nebuchadnezzar, and his politics, and the methods of his government, and the ministers he employed, and thought himself wiser than he; and therefore his mother harps upon that. "<hi type="italic">The king,</hi> I say, <hi type="italic">thy father,</hi> to whose good management all thou hast owing, he pronounced him chief of, and gave him dominion over, all the wise men of Babylon, and <hi type="italic">named him Belteshazzar,</hi> according to the name of his god, thinking thereby to put honour upon him;" but Daniel, by constantly making use of his Jewish name himself (which he resolved to keep, in token of his faithful adherence to his religion), had worn out that name; only the queen-dowager remembered it, otherwise he was generally called <hi type="italic">Daniel.</hi> Note, It is a very good office to revive the remembrance of the good services of worthy men, who are themselves modest, and willing that they should be forgotten. 3. The motion she makes concerning him: <hi type="italic">Let Daniel be called, and he will show the interpretation.</hi> By this it appears that Daniel was now forgotten at court. Belshazzar was a stranger to him, knew not that he had such a jewel in his kingdom. With the new king there came in a new ministry, and the old one was laid aside. Note, There are a great many valuable men, and such as might be made very useful, that lie long buried in obscurity, and some that have done eminent services that live to be overlooked and taken no notice of; but, whatever men are, God is not unrighteous to forget the services done to his kingdom. Daniel, being turned out of his place, lived privately, and sought not any opportunity to come into notice again; yet he lived near the court and within call, though Babylon was now besieged, that he might be ready, if there were occasion, to do any good office, by what interest he had among the great ones, for the children of his people. But Providence so ordered it that now, just at the fall of that monarchy, he should by the queen's means be brought to court again, that he might lie there ready for preferment in the ensuing government. Thus do <hi type="italic">the righteous shine forth out of obscurity,</hi> and <hi type="italic">before honour is humility.</hi> <div eID="gen19444" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19445" type="x-p"/> II. The introducing of Daniel to the king, and his request to him to read and expound the writing. Daniel was <hi type="italic">brought in before the king,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.6.13">v. 13</reference>. He was now nearly ninety years of age, so that his years, and honours, and former preferments, might have entitled him to a free admission into the king's presence; yet he was willing to be conducted in, as a stranger, by the master of the ceremonies. Note, 1. The king asks, with an air of haughtiness: <hi type="italic">Art thou that Daniel who art of the children of the captivity?</hi> Being a Jew, and a captive, he was loth to be beholden to him if he could help it. 2. He tells him what an encomium he had heard of him (<reference osisRef="Dan.6.14">v. 14</reference>), <hi type="italic">that the spirit of the gods was in him;</hi> and he had sent for him to try whether he deserved so high a character or no. 3. He acknowledges that all the wise men of Babylon were baffled; they could not <hi type="italic">read this writing,</hi> nor <hi type="italic">show the interpretation,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.6.16">v. 16</reference>. But, 4. He promises him the same rewards that he had promised them if he would do it, <reference osisRef="Dan.6.16">v. 16</reference>. It was strange that the magicians, when now, and in Nebuchadnezzar's time, once and again, they were nonplussed, did not attempt something to save their credit; if they had with a good assurance said, "This is the meaning of such a dream, such a writing," who could disprove them? But God so ordered it that they had nothing at all to say, as, when Christ was born, the heathen oracles were struck dumb. <div eID="gen19445" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19446" type="x-p"/> III. The interpretation which Daniel gave of these mystic characters, which was so far from easing the king of his fears that we may suppose it increased them rather. Daniel was now in years, and Belshazzar was young; and therefore he seems to take a greater liberty of dealing plainly and roundly with him than he had done upon the like occasions with Nebuchadnezzar. In reproving any man, especially great men, there is need of wisdom to consider all circumstances; for they are <hi type="italic">the reproofs of instruction</hi> that are <hi type="italic">the way of life.</hi> In Daniel's discourse here, <div eID="gen19446" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19447" type="x-p"/> 1. He undertakes to read the writing which gave them this alarm, and to show them the interpretation of it, <reference osisRef="Dan.6.17">v. 17</reference>. He slights the offer he made him of rewards, is not pleased that it was mentioned, for he is not one of those that <hi type="italic">divine for money;</hi> what gratuities Nebuchadnezzar gave him afterwards he gladly accepted, but he scorned to bargain for them, or to read the <hi type="italic">writing to the king</hi> for and in consideration of such and such honours promised him. No: "<hi type="italic">Let thy gifts be to thyself,</hi> for they will not be long thine, and <hi type="italic">give thy fee to another,</hi> to any of the wise men whom thou wouldst have most wished to earn it; I value it not." Daniel sees his kingdom now at its last gasp, and therefore looks with contempt upon his gifts and rewards. And thus should we despise all the gifts and rewards that this world can give did we see, as we may by faith, its final period hastening on. Let it give its perishing gifts to another; there are better gifts which we have our eyes and hearts upon; but let us do our duty in the world, do it all the real service we can, read God's writing to it in a profession of religion, and by an agreeable conversation make known the interpretation of it, and then trust God for his gifts, his rewards, in comparison with which all the world can give is mere trash and trifles. <div eID="gen19447" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19448" type="x-p"/> 2. He largely recounts to the king God's dealings with his father Nebuchadnezzar, which were intended for instruction and warning to him, <reference osisRef="Dan.6.18">v. 18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.6.21">21</reference>. This is not intended for a flourish or an amusement, but is a necessary preliminary to the interpretation of the writing. Note, That we may understand aright what God is doing with us, it is of use to us to review what he has done with others. <div eID="gen19448" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19449" type="x-p"/> (1.) He describes the great dignity and power to which the divine Providence had advanced Nebuchadnezzar, <reference osisRef="Dan.6.18-Dan.6.19">v. 18, 19</reference>. He had <hi type="italic">a kingdom, and majesty, and glory, and honour,</hi> for aught we know, above what any heathen prince ever had before him; he thought that he got his glory by his own extraordinary conduct and courage, and ascribed his successes to a projecting active genius of his own; but Daniel tells him who now enjoyed what he had laboured for that it was the <hi type="italic">most high God, the God of gods and Lord of kings</hi> (as Nebuchadnezzar himself had called him), that gave him <hi type="italic">that kingdom,</hi> that vast dominion, that majesty wherewith he presided in the affairs of it, and that <hi type="italic">glory and honour</hi> which by his prosperous management he acquired. Note, Whatever degree of outward prosperity any arrive at, they must own that it is of God's giving, not their own getting. Let it never be said, <hi type="italic">My might,</hi> and <hi type="italic">the power of my hand, have gotten me this wealth,</hi> this preferment; but let it always be remembered that it is <hi type="italic">God that gives men power to get wealth,</hi> and gives success to their endeavours. Now the power which God gave to Nebuchadnezzar is here described to be very great in respect both of ability and of authority. [1.] His ability was so strong that it was irresistible; such was the majesty that God gave him, so numerous were the forces he had at command, and such an admirable dexterity he had at commanding them, that, which way soever his sword turned, it prospered. He could captivate and subdue nations by threatening them, without striking a stroke, for <hi type="italic">all people trembled and feared before him,</hi> and would compound with him for their lives upon any terms. See what force is, and what the fear of it does. It is that by which the brutal part of the world, even of the world of mankind, both governs and is governed. [2.] His authority was so absolute that it was uncontrollable. The power which was allowed him, which descended upon him, or which, at least, he assumed, was without contradiction, was absolute and despotic, none shared with him either in the legislative or in the executive part of it. In dispensing punishments he condemned or acquitted at pleasure: <hi type="italic">Whom he would he slew, and whom he would he saved alive,</hi> though both were equally innocent or equally guilty. The <hi type="italic">jus vitæ et necis—the power of life and death</hi> was entirely in his hand. In dispensing rewards he granted or denied preferment at pleasure: <hi type="italic">Whom he would he set up, and whom he would he put down,</hi> merely for a humour, and without giving a reason so much as to himself; but it is all <hi type="italic">ex mero motu—of his own good pleasure,</hi> and <hi type="italic">stat pro ratione voluntas—his will stands for a reason.</hi> Such was the constitution of the eastern monarchies, such the manner of their kings. <div eID="gen19449" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19450" type="x-p"/> (2.) He sets before him the sins which Nebuchadnezzar had been guilty of, whereby he had provoked God against him. [1.] He behaved insultingly towards those that were under him, and grew tyrannical and oppressive. The description given of his power intimates his abuse of his power, and that he was directed in what he did by humour and passion, not by reason and equity; so that he often condemned the innocent and acquitted the guilty, both which are an <hi type="italic">abomination to the Lord.</hi> He deposed men of merit and preferred unworthy men, to the great detriment of the public, and for this he was accountable to the most high God, that gave him his power. Note, It is a very hard and rare thing for men to have an absolute arbitrary power, and not to make an ill use of it. Camden has a distich of Giraldus, wherein he speaks of it as a rare instance, concerning our king Henry II of England, that never any man had so much power and did so little hurt with it. <div eID="gen19450" type="x-p"/> <lg sID="gen19451"/> <l level="1" sID="gen19452"/>Glorior hoc uno, quod nunquam vidimus unum,<l eID="gen19452" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen19453"/>Nec potuisse magis, nec nocuisse minus—<l eID="gen19453" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen19454"/>Of him I can say, exulting, that with the same power<l eID="gen19454" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen19455"/>to do harm no one was ever more inoffensive.<l eID="gen19455" level="1"/> <lg eID="gen19451"/> <div sID="gen19456" type="x-p"/> But that was not all. [2.] He behaved insolently towards the God above him, and grew proud and haughty (<reference osisRef="Dan.6.20">v. 20</reference>): <hi type="italic">His heart was lifted up,</hi> and there his sin and ruin began; his <hi type="italic">mind was hardened</hi> in pride, hardened against the commands of God and his judgments; he was willful and obstinate, and neither the word of God nor his rod made any lasting impression upon him. Note, Pride is a sin that hardens the heart in all other sins and renders the means of repentance and reformation ineffectual. <div eID="gen19456" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19457" type="x-p"/> (3.) He reminds him of the judgments of God that were brought upon him for his pride and obstinacy, how he was deprived of his reason, and so <hi type="italic">deposed from his kingly throne</hi> (<reference osisRef="Dan.6.20">v. 20</reference>), <hi type="italic">driven from among men,</hi> to <hi type="italic">dwell with the wild asses,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.6.21">v. 21</reference>. He that would not govern his subjects by rules of reason had not reason sufficient for the government himself. Note, Justly does God deprive men of their reason when they become unreasonable and will not use it, and of their power when they become oppressive and use it ill. He continued like a brute till <hi type="italic">he knew</hi> and embraced that first principle of religion, <hi type="italic">That the most high God rules.</hi> And it is rather by religion than reason that man is distinguished from, and dignified above, the beasts; and it is more his honour to be a subject to the supreme Creator than to be lord of the inferior creatures. Note, Kings must know, or shall be made to know, that the most high God rules in their kingdoms (that is an <hi type="italic">imperium in imperio—an empire within an empire,</hi> not to be excepted against), and that he appoints over them whomsoever he will. As he makes heirs, so he makes princes. <div eID="gen19457" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19458" type="x-p"/> 3. In God's name, he exhibits articles of impeachment against Belshazzar. Before he reads him his doom, from the hand-writing on the wall, he shows him his crime, that God may be <hi type="italic">justified when he speaks, and clear when he judges.</hi> Now that which he lays to his charge is, (1.) That he had not taken warning by the judgments of God upon his father (<reference osisRef="Dan.6.22">v. 22</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou his son, O Belshazzar! hast not humbled thy heart, though thou knewest all this.</hi> Note, It is a great offence to God if our hearts be not humbled before him to comply both with his precepts and with his providences, humbled by repentance, obedience, and patience; nay, he expects from the greatest of men that their hearts should be humbled before him, by an acknowledgment that, great as they are, to him they are accountable. And it is a great aggravation of the unhumbledness of our hearts when we know enough to humble them but do not consider and improve it, particularly when we know how others have been broken that would not bend, how others have fallen that would not stoop, and yet we continue stiff and inflexible. It makes the sin of children the more heinous if they tread in the steps of their parents' wickedness, though they have seen how dearly it has cost them, and how pernicious the consequences of it have been. Do we know this, do we know all this, and yet are we not humbled? (2.) That he had affronted God more impudently than Nebuchadnezzar himself had done, witness the revels of this very night, in the midst of which he was seized with this horror (<reference osisRef="Dan.6.23">v. 23</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Thou hast lifted up thyself against the Lord of heaven,</hi> hast swelled with rage against him, and taken up arms against his crown and dignity, in this particular instance, that thou hast profaned the <hi type="italic">vessels of his house,</hi> and made the utensils of his sanctuary instruments of thy iniquity, and, in an actual designed contempt of him, hast <hi type="italic">praised the gods of silver and gold, which see not, nor hear, nor know</hi> anything, as if they were to be preferred before the God that sees, and hears, and knows every thing." Sinners that are resolved to go on in sin are well enough pleased with gods that <hi type="italic">neither see, nor hear, nor know,</hi> for then they may sin securely; but they will find, to their confusion, that though those are the gods they choose those are not the gods they must be judged by, but one to whom <hi type="italic">all things are naked and open.</hi> (3.) That he had not answered the end of his creation and maintenance: <hi type="italic">The God in whose hand thy breath is, and whose are all thy ways, hast thou not glorified.</hi> This is a general charge, which stands good against us all; let us consider how we shall answer it. Observe, [1.] Our dependence upon God as our creator, preserver, benefactor, owner, and ruler; not only from his hand our breath was at first, but <hi type="italic">in his hand our breath is</hi> still; it is he that <hi type="italic">holds our souls in life,</hi> and, if he <hi type="italic">take away our breath, we die.</hi> Our times being <hi type="italic">in his hand,</hi> so is our breath, by which our times are measured. <hi type="italic">In him we live, and move, and have our being;</hi> we live by him, live upon him, and cannot live without him. <hi type="italic">The way of man is not in himself,</hi> not at his own command, at his own disposal, <hi type="italic">but his are all our ways;</hi> for our hearts are in his hand, and so are the hearts of all men, even of kings, who seem to act most as free-agents. [2.] Our duty to God, in consideration of this dependence; we ought to glorify him, to devote ourselves to his honour and employ ourselves in his service, to make it our care to please him and our business to praise him. [3.] Our default in this duty, notwithstanding that dependence; we have not done it; for we have <hi type="italic">all sinned, and come short of the glory of God.</hi> This is the indictment against Belshazzar; there needs no proof, it is made good by the notorious evidence of the fact, and his own conscience cannot but plead guilty to it. And therefore, <div eID="gen19458" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19459" type="x-p"/> 4. He now proceeds to read the sentence, as he found it <hi type="italic">written upon the wall: "Then</hi>" (says Daniel) "when thou hast come to such a height of impiety as thus to trample upon the most sacred things, <hi type="italic">then</hi> when thou wast in the midst of thy sacrilegious idolatrous feast, then was <hi type="italic">the part of the hand,</hi> the writing fingers, sent <hi type="italic">from him,</hi> from that God whom thou didst so daringly affront, and who had borne so long with thee, but would bear no longer; he <hi type="italic">sent them,</hi> and <hi type="italic">this writing,</hi> thou now seest, <hi type="italic">was written,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.6.24">v. 24</reference>. It is he that now <hi type="italic">writes bitter things against thee,</hi> and <hi type="italic">makes thee to possess thy iniquities,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Job.13.26">Job xiii. 26</reference>. Note, As the sin of sinners is written in the book of God's omniscience, so the doom of sinners is written in the book of God's law; and the day is coming when those <hi type="italic">books shall be opened,</hi> and they shall be judged by them. Now the writing was, <hi type="italic">Mene, Mene, Tekel, Upharsin,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.6.25">v. 25</reference>. It is well that we have an authentic exposition of these words annexed, else we could make little of them, so concise are they; the signification of them is, <hi type="italic">He has numbered, he has weighed, and they divide.</hi> The Chaldean wise men, because they knew not that there is but one God only, could not understand who this <hi type="italic">He</hi> should be, and for that reason (some think) the writing puzzled them. (1.) <hi type="italic">Mene;</hi> that is repeated, for the thing is certain—<hi type="italic">Mene, mene;</hi> that signifies, both in Hebrew and Chaldee, <hi type="italic">He has numbered and finished,</hi> which Daniel explains thus (<reference osisRef="Dan.6.26">v. 26</reference>): "<hi type="italic">God has numbered thy kingdom,</hi> the years and days of the continuance of it; these were numbered in the counsel of God, and now they are finished; the term has expired for and during which thou wast to hold it, and now it must be surrendered. Here is an end of thy kingdom." (2.) <hi type="italic">Tekel;</hi> that signifies, in Chaldee, <hi type="italic">Thou art weighed,</hi> and, in Hebrew, <hi type="italic">Thou art too light.</hi> So Dr. Lightfoot. For this king and his actions are weighed in the just and unerring balances of divine equity. God does as perfectly know his true character as the goldsmith knows the weight of that which he has weighed in the nicest scales. God does not give judgment against him till he has first pondered his actions, and considered the merits of his case. "But thou art <hi type="italic">found wanting,</hi> unworthy to have such a trust lodged in thee, a vain, light, empty man, a man of no weight or consideration." (3.) <hi type="italic">Upharsin,</hi> which should be rendered, <hi type="italic">and Pharsin,</hi> or <hi type="italic">Peres.</hi> <hi type="italic">Parsin,</hi> in Hebrew, signifies the <hi type="italic">Persians; Paresin,</hi> in Chaldee, signifies <hi type="italic">dividing;</hi> Daniel puts both together (<reference osisRef="Dan.6.28">v. 28</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Thy kingdom is divided,</hi> is rent from thee, and <hi type="italic">given to the Medes and Persians,</hi> as a prey to be divided among them." Now this may, without any force, be applied to the doom of sinners. <hi type="italic">Mene, Tekel, Peres,</hi> may easily be made to signify <hi type="italic">death, judgment,</hi> and <hi type="italic">hell.</hi> At death, the sinner's days are <hi type="italic">numbered</hi> and <hi type="italic">finished;</hi> after death the judgment, when he will be <hi type="italic">weighed in the balance and found wanting;</hi> and after judgment the sinner will be <hi type="italic">cut asunder,</hi> and given as a prey to the devil and his angels. Daniel does not here give Belshazzar such advice and encouragement to repent as he had given Nebuchadnezzar, because he saw the decree had gone forth and he would not be allowed any space to repent. <div eID="gen19459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19460" type="x-p"/> One would have thought that Belshazzar would be exasperated against Daniel, and, seeing his own case desperate, would be in a rage against him. But he was so far convicted by his own conscience of the reasonableness of all he said that he objected nothing against it; but, on the contrary, gave Daniel the reward he promised him, put on him the <hi type="italic">scarlet gown</hi> and the <hi type="italic">gold chain,</hi> and proclaimed him the <hi type="italic">third ruler in the kingdom</hi> (<reference osisRef="Dan.6.29">v. 29</reference>), because he would be as good as his word, and because it was not Daniel's fault if the exposition of the hand-writing was not such as he desired. Note, Many show great respect to God's prophets who yet have no regard to his word. Daniel did not value these titles and ensigns of honour, yet would not refuse them, because they were tokens of his prince's good-will: but we have reason to think that he received them with a smile, foreseeing how soon they would all wither with him that bestowed them. They were like Jonah's gourd, which came up in a night and perished in a night, and therefore it was folly for him to be <hi type="italic">exceedingly glad</hi> of them.
entries.46a3204c3083b10b2ca26cc7d627a20ce58bedea: <div eID="gen19460" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Daniel Deals Plainly with Belshazzar; Interpreting of the Writing on the Wall. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi>  538.)</title> <div sID="gen19461" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">30</hi> In that night was Belshazzar the king of the Chaldeans slain. <hi type="super">31</hi> And Darius the Median took the kingdom, <hi type="italic">being</hi> about threescore and two years old. <div eID="gen19461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19462" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The death of the king. Reason enough he had to tremble, for he was just falling into the hands of the <hi type="italic">king of terrors,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.6.30">v. 30</reference>. <hi type="italic">In that night,</hi> when his heart was merry with wine, the besiegers broke into the city, aimed at the palace; there they found the king, and gave him his death's wound. He could not find any place so secret as to conceal him, or so strong as to protect him. Heathen writers speak of Cyrus's taking Babylon by surprise, with the assistance of two deserters that showed him the best way into the city. And it was foretold what a consternation it would be to the court, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.11">Jer. li. 11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.39">39</reference>. Note, Death comes as a snare upon those whose hearts are overcharged with surfeiting and drunkenness. 2. The transferring of the kingdom into other hands. From the head of gold we now descend to the breast and arms of silver. <hi type="italic">Darius the Mede took the kingdom</hi> in partnership with, and by the consent of, Cyrus, who had conquered it, <reference osisRef="Dan.6.31">v. 31</reference>. They were partners in war and conquest, and so they were in dominion, <reference osisRef="Dan.6.28">ch. vi. 28</reference>. Notice is taken of his age, that he was now sixty-two years old, for which reason Cyrus, who was his nephew, gave him the precedency. Some observe that being now sixty-two years old, in the last year of the captivity, he was born in the eighth year of it, and that was the year when Jeconiah was carried captive and all the nobles, &c. See <reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.13-2Kgs.24.15">2 Kings xxiv. 13-15</reference>. Just at that time when the most fatal stroke was given was a prince born that in process of time should avenge Jerusalem upon Babylon, and heal the wound that was now given. Thus deep are the counsels of God concerning his people, thus kind are his designs towards them.  <chapter eID="Dan.5"/> <div eID="gen19462" type="x-p"/>

entries.32bfa5692cdd6b9c78aa309a8a07cce7a6b492a1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12039"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 5</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Dan.5.1-Dan.5.31">Da 5:1-31</reference>. Belshazzar's Impious Feast; the Handwriting on the Wall Interpreted by Daniel of the Doom of Babylon and Its King.</title> <div sID="gen21768" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12039"/><hi type="bold">1. Belshazzar--</hi>Rawlinson, from the Assyrian inscriptions, has explained the seeming discrepancy between Daniel and the heathen historians of Babylon, Berosus and Abydenus, who say the last king (Nabonidus) surrendered in Borsippa, after Babylon was taken, and had an honorable abode in Caramania assigned to him. Belshazzar was joint king with his father (called Minus in the inscriptions), but subordinate to him; hence the Babylonian account suppresses the facts which cast discredit on Babylon, namely, that Belshazzar shut himself up in that city and fell at its capture; while it records the surrender of the principal king in Borsippa (see my Introduction to Daniel). The heathen Xenophon's description of Belshazzar accords with Daniel's; he calls him "impious," and illustrates his cruelty by mentioning that he killed one of his nobles, merely because, in hunting, the noble struck down the game before him; and unmanned a courtier, Gadates, at a banquet, because one of the king's concubines praised him as handsome. Daniel shows none of the sympathy for him which he had for Nebuchadnezzar. Xenophon confirms Daniel as to Belshazzar's end. Winer explains the "shazzar" in the name as meaning "fire."<div eID="gen21768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21769" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">made ... feast--</hi>heaven-sent infatuation when his city was at the time being besieged by Cyrus. The fortifications and abundant provisions in the city made the king despise the besiegers. It was a festival day among the Babylonians [Xenophon].<div eID="gen21769" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21770" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">drank ... before the thousand--</hi>The king, on this extraordinary occasion, departed from his usual way of feasting apart from his nobles (compare <reference osisRef="Esth.1.3">Es 1:3</reference>). <div eID="gen21770" type="x-p"/>
entries.352a24bc722f64646f89996647849a0c8e97c4c4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12040"/><div sID="gen21771" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12040"/><hi type="bold">2. whiles he tasted the wine--</hi>While under the effects of wine, men will do what they dare not do when sober.<div eID="gen21771" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21772" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his father Nebuchadnezzar--</hi>that is, his forefather. So "Jesus ... the son of David, the son of Abraham" (<reference osisRef="Matt.1.1">Mt 1:1</reference>). Daniel does not say that the other kings mentioned in other writers did not reign between Belshazzar and Nebuchadnezzar, namely, Evil-merodach (<reference osisRef="Jer.52.31">Jr 52:31</reference>), Neriglissar, his brother-in-law, and Laborasoarchod (nine months). Berosus makes Nabonidus, the last king, to have been one of the people, raised to the throne by an insurrection. As the inscriptions show that Belshazzar was distinct from, and joint king with, him, this is not at variance with Daniel, whose statement that Belshazzar was son (grandson) of Nebuchadnezzar is corroborated by Jeremiah (<reference osisRef="Jer.27.7">Jr 27:7</reference>). Their joint, yet independent, testimony, as contemporaries, and having the best means of information, is more trustworthy than any of the heathen historians, if there were a discrepancy. Evil-merodach, son of Nebuchadnezzar (according to Berosus), reigned but a short time (one or two years), having, in consequence of his bad government, been dethroned by a plot of Neriglissar, his sister's husband; hence Daniel does not mention him. At the elevation of Nabonidus as supreme king, Belshazzar, the grandson of Nebuchadnezzar, was doubtless suffered to be subordinate king and successor, in order to conciliate the legitimate party. Thus the seeming discrepancy becomes a confirmation of genuineness when cleared up, for the real harmony must have been undesigned.<div eID="gen21772" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21773" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wives ... concubines--</hi>not usually present at feasts in the East, where women of the harem are kept in strict seclusion. Hence Vashti's refusal to appear at Ahasuerus' feast (<reference osisRef="Esth.1.9-Esth.1.12">Es 1:9-12</reference>). But the Babylonian court, in its reckless excesses, seems not to have been so strict as the Persian. Xenophon [Cyropædia, 5.2,28] confirms Daniel, representing a feast of Belshazzar where the concubines are present. At the beginning "the lords" (<reference osisRef="Dan.5.1">Da 5:1</reference>), for whom the feast was made, alone seem to have been present; but as the revelry advanced, the women were introduced. Two classes of them are mentioned, those to whom belonged the privileges of "wives," and those strictly concubines (<reference osisRef="2Sam.5.13">2Sa 5:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.3">1Ki 11:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Song.6.8">So 6:8</reference>). <div eID="gen21773" type="x-p"/>

This act was not one of necessity, or for honor's sake, but in reckless profanity. <div eID="gen21774" type="x-p"/>
entries.839f99badda5df010304e296d1485ad1174311b4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12042"/><div sID="gen21775" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12042"/><hi type="bold">4. praised--</hi>sang and shouted praises to "gods," which being of gold, "are their own witnesses" (<reference osisRef="Isa.44.9">Is 44:9</reference>), confuting the folly of those who fancy such to be gods. <div eID="gen21775" type="x-p"/>
entries.54d06f63a5d20538a336f628478a9449304867bd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12043"/><div sID="gen21776" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12043"/><hi type="bold">5. In the same hour--</hi>that the cause of God's visitation might be palpable, namely, the profanation of His vessels and His holy name.<div eID="gen21776" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21777" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fingers of ... hand--</hi>God admonishes him, not by a dream (as Nebuchadnezzar had been warned), or by a voice, but by "fingers coming forth," the invisibility of Him who moved them heightening the awful impressiveness of the scene, the hand of the Unseen One attesting his doom before the eyes of himself and his guilty fellow revellers.<div eID="gen21777" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21778" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">against the candlestick--</hi>the candelabra; where the mystic characters would be best seen. Barnes makes it the candlestick taken from the temple of Jerusalem, the nearness of the writing to it intimating that the rebuke was directed against the sacrilege.<div eID="gen21778" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21779" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">upon the plaster of the wall of the king's palace--</hi>Written in cuneiform letters on slabs on the walls, and on the very bricks, are found the perpetually recurring recital of titles, victories, and exploits, to remind the spectator at every point of the regal greatness. It is significant, that on the same wall on which the king was accustomed to read the flattering legends of his own magnificence, he beholds the mysterious inscription which foretells his fall (compare <reference osisRef="Prov.16.18">Pr 16:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.12.21-Acts.12.23">Ac 12:21-23</reference>).<div eID="gen21779" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21780" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">part of the hand--</hi>the anterior part, namely, the fingers. <div eID="gen21780" type="x-p"/>
entries.1f26d711ee7c000dc9677c653a7c664ebea5cad3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12044"/><div sID="gen21781" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12044"/><hi type="bold">6. countenance--</hi>literally, "brightness," that is, his bright look.<div eID="gen21781" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21782" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">joints of his loins--</hi>"the vertebræ of his back" [Gesenius]. <div eID="gen21782" type="x-p"/>
entries.43c1c3ef23472f54d90bab96699b17c63719f397: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12045"/><div sID="gen21783" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12045"/>7. He calls for the magicians, who more than once had been detected in imposture. He neglects God, and Daniel, whose fame as an interpreter was then well-established. The world wishes to be deceived and shuts its eyes against the light [Calvin]. The Hebrews think the words were Chaldee, but in the old Hebrew character (like that now in the Samaritan Pentateuch).<div eID="gen21783" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21784" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">third ruler--</hi>The first place was given to the king; the second, to the son of the king, or of the queen; the third, to the chief of the satraps. <div eID="gen21784" type="x-p"/>
entries.4dda79e0534c8759509f9fe48908602bd2659605: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12046"/><div sID="gen21785" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12046"/>8. The words were in such a character as to be illegible to the Chaldees, God reserving this honor to Daniel. <div eID="gen21785" type="x-p"/>
entries.dbe3919c8b1b05b3b68104feaebda81dfa91e904: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12047"/><div sID="gen21786" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12047"/><hi type="bold">10. queen--</hi>the queen mother, or grandmother, Nitocris, had not been present till now. She was wife either of Nebuchadnezzar or of Evil merodach; hence her acquaintance with the services of Daniel. She completed the great works which the former had begun. Hence Herodotus attributes them to her alone. This accounts for the deference paid to her by Belshazzar. (See on <reference osisRef="Dan.4.36">Da 4:36</reference>). Compare similar rank given to the queen mother among the Hebrews (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.13">1Ki 15:13</reference>). <div eID="gen21786" type="x-p"/>
entries.e7c4a8ce5a490bf87f0a8658fb95f7385780f292: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12048"/><div sID="gen21787" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12048"/><hi type="bold">11. spirit of the holy gods--</hi>She remembers and repeats Nebuchadnezzar's language (<reference osisRef="Dan.4.8">Da 4:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.9.18">9, 18</reference>). As Daniel was probably, according to Oriental custom, deprived of the office to which Nebuchadnezzar had promoted him, as "master of the magicians" (<reference osisRef="Dan.4.9">Da 4:9</reference>), at the king's death, Belshazzar might easily be ignorant of his services.<div eID="gen21787" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21788" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the king ... thy father the king ... thy father--</hi>The repetition marks with emphatic gravity both the excellencies of Daniel, and the fact that Nebuchadnezzar, whom Belshazzar is bound to reverence as his father, had sought counsel from him in similar circumstances. <div eID="gen21788" type="x-p"/>
entries.930cdf82069698c2338f9e6998c80d494dc46df4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12049"/><div sID="gen21789" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12049"/><hi type="bold">13. the captivity of Judah--</hi>the captive Jews residing in Babylon. <div eID="gen21789" type="x-p"/>
entries.e4c4ae4507994cbc34d23f0b93e5e526c3c4ecbc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12050"/><div sID="gen21790" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12050"/>17. Not inconsistent with <reference osisRef="Dan.5.29">Da 5:29</reference>. For here he declares his interpretation of the words is not from the desire of reward. The honors in <reference osisRef="Dan.5.29">Da 5:29</reference> were doubtless urged on him, without his wish, in such a way that he could not with propriety refuse them. Had he refused them after announcing the doom of the kingdom, he might have been suspected of cowardice or treason. <div eID="gen21790" type="x-p"/>
entries.e14c5152be33279da5d38257e57e4aa98c910499: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12051"/><div sID="gen21791" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12051"/><hi type="bold">18. God gave--</hi>It was not his own birth or talents which gave him the vast empire, as he thought. To make him unlearn his proud thought was the object of God's visitation on him.<div eID="gen21791" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21792" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">majesty--</hi>in the eyes of his subjects.<div eID="gen21792" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21793" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">glory--</hi>from his victories.<div eID="gen21793" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21794" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">honour--</hi>from the enlargement and decoration of the city. <div eID="gen21794" type="x-p"/>
entries.d726f19717f40cdf80d824120e560404c07ee65f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12052"/><div sID="gen21795" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12052"/>19. entries.b574970367e796ce5210f3fd27f379e70eb61d9c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12053"/><div sID="gen21796" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12053"/><hi type="bold">21. heart was made like ... beasts--</hi>literally, "he made his heart like the beasts," that is, he desired to dwell with them. <div eID="gen21796" type="x-p"/>
entries.8dccb1de904019fbf3f83bca3b46ab342533218b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12054"/><div sID="gen21797" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12054"/>22. entries.84902703a49b838e9ca26f587bd236fe2b8a560b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12056"/><div sID="gen21799" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12056"/><hi type="bold">24. Then--</hi>When thou liftedst up thyself against the Lord.<div eID="gen21799" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21800" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the part of the hand--</hi>the fore part, the fingers.<div eID="gen21800" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21801" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">was ... sent from him--</hi>that is, from God. <div eID="gen21801" type="x-p"/>
entries.e97a184000ebeee8938712f18221daf78a189e7b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12057"/><div sID="gen21802" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12057"/><hi type="bold">25. Mene, Mene, Tekel, Upharsin--</hi>literally, "numbered, weighed, and dividers." <div eID="gen21802" type="x-p"/>
entries.4351889efa87a16ebaeb2cc6bff97e7b2f47a19e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12058"/><div sID="gen21803" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12058"/>26. God hath fixed the number of years of thine empire, and that number is now complete. <div eID="gen21803" type="x-p"/>
entries.8840b3c1c7fe9f51d71c960bfdb2f594d2400fbf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12059"/><div sID="gen21804" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12059"/><hi type="bold">27. weighed in the balances--</hi>The Egyptians thought that Osiris weighed the actions of the dead in a literal balance. The Babylonians may have had the same notion, which would give a peculiar appropriateness to the image here used.<div eID="gen21804" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21805" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">found wanting--</hi>too light before God, the weigher of actions (<reference osisRef="1Sam.2.3">1Sa 2:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.62.9">Psa 62:9</reference>). Like spurious gold or silver (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.30">Jr 6:30</reference>). <div eID="gen21805" type="x-p"/>
entries.fdb6bcb0f32d741592a903740ea38b18f48a0021: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12060"/><div sID="gen21806" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12060"/><hi type="bold">28. Peres--</hi>the explanation of "dividers" (<reference osisRef="Dan.5.25">Da 5:25</reference>), the active participle plural there being used for the passive participle singular, "dividers" for "divided." The word "Peres" alludes to the similar word "Persia."<div eID="gen21806" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21807" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">divided--</hi>namely, among the Medes and Persians [Maurer]; or, "severed" from thee [Grotius]. <div eID="gen21807" type="x-p"/>
entries.48b74cbe9b46b5102a5c588c35177b06201c9bb9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12061"/><div sID="gen21808" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12061"/><hi type="bold">29. Belshazzar ... clothed Daniel with scarlet--</hi>To come from the presence of a prince in a dress presented to the wearer as a distinction is still held a great honor in the East. Daniel was thus restored to a similar rank to what he had held under Nebuchadnezzar (<reference osisRef="Dan.2.48">Da 2:48</reference>). Godly fidelity which might be expected to bring down vengeance, as in this case, is often rewarded even in this life. The king, having promised, was ashamed before his courtiers to break his word. He perhaps also affected to despise the prophecy of his doom, as an idle threat. As to Daniel's reasons for now accepting what at first he had declined, compare Note, see on <reference osisRef="Dan.5.17">Da 5:17</reference>. The insignia of honor would be witnesses for God's glory to the world of his having by God's aid interpreted the mystic characters. The cause of his elevation too would secure the favor of the new dynasty (<reference osisRef="Dan.6.2">Da 6:2</reference>) for both himself and his captive countrymen. As the capture of the city by Cyrus was not till near daylight, there was no want of time in that eventful night for accomplishing all that is here recorded. The capture of the city so immediately after the prophecy of it (following Belshazzar's sacrilege), marked most emphatically to the whole world the connection between Babylon's sin and its punishment. <div eID="gen21808" type="x-p"/>
entries.7adc50d9e58029245fa8ba5b92ef30ee1e5f76ce: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12062"/><div sID="gen21809" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12062"/>30. Herodotus and Xenophon confirm Daniel as to the suddenness of the event. Cyrus diverted the Euphrates into a new channel and, guided by two deserters, marched by the dry bed into the city, while the Babylonians were carousing at an annual feast to the gods. See also <reference osisRef="Isa.21.5">Is 21:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.44.27">44:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.50.38">Jr 50:38</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.50.39">39</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.51.36">51:36</reference>. As to Belshazzar's being slain, compare Is 14:18-20; 21:2-9; Jr 50:29-35; 51:57. <div eID="gen21809" type="x-p"/>
entries.ae2de05b7e3d3cf9a8a402fb0f09e157ed987a62: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12063"/><div sID="gen21810" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12063"/><hi type="bold">31. Darius the Median--</hi>that is, Cyaxares II, the son and successor of Astyages, 569-536 B.C. Though Koresh, or Cyrus, was leader of the assault, yet all was done in the name of Darius; therefore, he alone is mentioned here; but <reference osisRef="Dan.6.28">Da 6:28</reference> shows Daniel was not ignorant of Cyrus' share in the capture of Babylon. <reference osisRef="Isa.13.17">Is 13:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.21.2">21:2</reference>, confirm Daniel in making the Medes the leading nation in destroying Babylon. So also <reference osisRef="Jer.51.11">Jr 51:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.28">28</reference>. Herodotus, on the other hand, omits mentioning Darius, as that king, being weak and sensual, gave up all the authority to his energetic nephew, Cyrus [Xenophon, Cyropædia, 1.5; 8.7].<div eID="gen21810" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21811" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">threescore and two years old--</hi>This agrees with Xenophon [Cyropædia, 8.5,19], as to Cyaxares II.  <chapter eID="Dan.5"/>

entries.b6e9e39e15f257d216a3e04ad37e266a35677a78: <div eID="gen32994" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen32995" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen32996" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen32996" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen32995" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen32997" type="x-p"/> In the commencement of this chapter we are informed how Belshazzar, the grandson of Nebuchadnezzar, when rioting in his palace, and profaning the severed vessels of the temple, <reference osisRef="Dan.5.1-Dan.5.4">Dan 5:1-4</reference>, was suddenly terrified with the appearance of the fingers of a man's hand, which wrote a few words on the wall before him, <reference osisRef="Dan.5.5">Dan 5:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.5.6">Dan 5:6</reference>. The wise men and astrologers were immediately called in to show the king the interpretation; but they could not so much as read the writing, because (as Houbigant and others have conjectured) though the words are in the Chaldee tongue, yet they were written in the Samaritan or ancient Hebrew characters, with which the wise men of Babylon were very probably unacquainted, as the Jews were at that time a despised people, and the knowledge of their language not a fashionable attainment, <reference osisRef="Dan.5.7-Dan.5.9">Dan 5:7-9</reference>. Daniel, who had been so highly esteemed by Nebuchadnezzar for his superior wisdom, appears to have been altogether unknown to Belshazzar, till the queen (the same who had been the wife of Nebuchadnezzar according to the general opinion, or the queen consort according to others) had informed him, <reference osisRef="Dan.5.10-Dan.5.12">Dan 5:10-12</reference>. Upon the queen's recommendation, Daniel is called in, <reference osisRef="Dan.5.13-Dan.5.16">Dan 5:13-16</reference>; who boldly tells this despotic king, that as he had not benefited by the judgments inflicted on his grandfather, but gave himself up to pride and profanity, and had added to his other sins an utter contempt for the God of the Jews by drinking wine out of the sacred vessels of Jehovah in honor of his idols, <reference osisRef="Dan.5.17-Dan.5.23">Dan 5:17-23</reference>; the Supreme Being, the Ruler of heaven and earth, had written his condemnation in three words, Mene, Tekel, Peres, <reference osisRef="Dan.5.24">Dan 5:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.5.25">Dan 5:25</reference>; the first of which is repeated in the copies containing the Chaldean original; but all the ancient Versions, except the Syriac, are without this repetition. Daniel then gives the king and his lords the fearful import of the writing, viz., that the period allotted for the duration of the Chaldean empire was now completed, (see <reference osisRef="Jer.25.12-Jer.25.14">Jer 25:12-14</reference>), and that the kingdom was about to be transferred to the Medes and Persians, <reference osisRef="Dan.5.26-Dan.5.28">Dan 5:26-28</reference>. However unwelcome such an interpretation must have been to Belshazzar, yet the monarch, overwhelmed with its clearness and certainty, commanded the prophet to be honored, <reference osisRef="Dan.5.29">Dan 5:29</reference>. And that very night the prediction was fulfilled, for the king was slain, <reference osisRef="Dan.5.30">Dan 5:30</reference>, and the city taken by the Medes and Persians, <reference osisRef="Dan.5.31">Dan 5:31</reference>. This great event was also predicted by Isaiah and Jeremiah; and the manner in which it was accomplished is recorded by Herodotus and Xenophon. <div eID="gen32997" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32998" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen32998" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32999" type="x-p"/> Belshazzar the king made a great feast - This chapter is out of its place, and should come in after the seventh and eighth. There are difficulties in the chronology. After the death of Nebuchadnezzar, Evil-merodach his son ascended the throne of Babylon. Having reigned about two years, he was slain by his brother-in-law, Neriglissar. He reigned four years, and was succeeded by his son Laborosoarchod, who reigned only nine months. At his death Belshazzar the son of Evil-merodach, was raised to the throne, and reigned seventeen years, and was slain, as we read here, by Cyrus, who surprised and took the city on the night of this festivity. This is the chronology on which Archbishop Usher, and other learned chronologists, agree; but the Scripture mentions only Nebuchadnezzar, Evil-merodach, and Belshazzar, by name; and Jeremiah, <reference osisRef="Jer.27.7">Jer 27:7</reference>, expressly says, "All nations shall serve him (Nebuchadnezzar), and his son (Evil-merodach), and his son's son (Belshazzar), until the very time of his land come;" i.e., till the time in which the empire should be seized by Cyrus. Here there is no mention of Neriglissar nor Laborosoarchod; but as they were usurpers, they might have been purposely passed by. But there remains one difficulty still: Belshazzar is expressly called the son of Nebuchadnezzar by the queen mother, <reference osisRef="Jer.27.11">Jer 27:11</reference> : "There is a man in thy kingdom, in whom is the spirit of the holy gods: and in the days of Thy Father light and understanding and wisdom, like the wisdom of the gods, was found in him: whom the king Nebuchadnezzar Thy Father, the king, I say, thy father, made master of the magicians." The solution of this difficulty is, that in Scripture the name of son is indifferently given to sons and grandsons, and even to great grandsons. And perhaps the repetition in the above verse may imply this: "The king, Nebuchadnezzar thy father, the king thy father." The king thy father's father, and consequently thy grandfather. If it have not some such meaning as this, it must be considered an idle repetition. As to the two other kings, Neriglissar and Laborosoarchod, mentioned by Josephus and Berosus, and by whom the chronology is so much puzzled, they might have been some petty kings, or viceroys, or satraps, who affected the kingdom, and produced disturbances, one for four years, and the other for nine months; and would in consequence not be acknowledged in the Babylonish chronology, nor by the sacred writers, any more than finally unsuccessful rebels are numbered among the kings of those nations which they have disturbed. I believe the only sovereigns we can acknowledge here are the following: <div eID="gen32999" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33000" type="x-p"/> 1. Nabopolassar; <div eID="gen33000" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33001" type="x-p"/> 2. Nebuchadnezzar; <div eID="gen33001" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33002" type="x-p"/> 3. Evil-merodach <div eID="gen33002" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33003" type="x-p"/> 4. Belshazzar; and with this last the Chaldean empire ended. <div eID="gen33003" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33004" type="x-p"/> To a thousand of his lords - Perhaps this means lords or satraps, that were each over one thousand men. But we learn from antiquity that the Persian kings were very profuse in their entertainments; but it does not follow that the Chaldeans were so too. Besides, one thousand lords and their appropriate attendants would have been very inconvenient in a nocturnal assembly. The text, however, supports the common translation. Literally, "Belshazzar the king made bread for his lords a thousand; and against the thousand he drank wine." That is, say some, he was a very great drinker.
entries.c97bee2205f721576d6f372f2f68f86683864d03: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen33004" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33005" type="x-p"/> Whiles he tasted the wine - He relished it, got heated by it, and when Wine got fully in, Wit went wholly out; and in consequence he acted the profane part of which we immediately read.
entries.e08561350730b89fcf62498ee3de8196443b9521: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen33005" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33006" type="x-p"/> And praised the gods of gold - They had gods of all sorts, and of all metals; with wooden gods, and stone gods, beside!
